items.title: 7.4 Rate law, rate constant and order of reaction

source_refs.note: Topic 7.4, printed page 154 (heading); the detail follows in 7.4.1 to 7.4.4.

blocks.text: The rate of a reaction at a given temperature may depend on the concentrations of one or more reactants and products.

blocks.alt: A banner with the general rate law rate = k [A]^x [B]^y. Left: the initial-rate table for the NO and H2 reaction with notes reading first order in H2 and second order in NO. Right: the hydrogen peroxide and iodide data with the calculation of k and the half-life formula. Bottom: a table of the units of k for orders 0 to 3 and a fractional order, with examples.
blocks.caption: Rate law, order of reaction and the units of the rate constant (original diagram after Tables 7.2 and 7.3 and the printed units derivation).
blocks.long_description: The exponents in the rate law come from experiment: doubling [H2] doubles the rate (first order) while doubling [NO] quadruples it (second order), so the reaction is third order overall. Dividing a measured initial rate by the concentrations gives k, 1.75 x 10^-2 dm3 mol-1 s-1 for the peroxide-iodide reaction, in which [H+] has no effect. The units of k follow from k = (mol dm-3)^(1-n) s-1: mol dm-3 s-1 for zero order, s-1 for first, dm3 mol-1 s-1 for second and dm6 mol-2 s-1 for third.
